lesson.title: After the Threat: How PTSD Keeps the Alarm On
lesson.summary: PTSD is a set of intrusion, avoidance, mood and cognition, and arousal symptoms that persist for more than a month after exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence.
lesson.body:
Post-traumatic stress disorder sits within the DSM's trauma and stressor related disorders, and it is unusual among psychological disorders because the diagnostic criteria explicitly require a specific kind of causal event, not just a symptom pattern. Criterion A specifies exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence, and it can occur in several ways: direct personal experience, witnessing the event happen to someone else in person, learning that it happened to a close family member or friend (in the case of actual or threatened death, it must have been violent or accidental), or repeated or extreme exposure to aversive details of the event, as can happen to first responders who repeatedly review details of traumatic cases as part of their work.

Beyond that exposure, PTSD requires symptoms from four distinct clusters. Intrusion symptoms include recurrent, involuntary, distressing memories of the event, nightmares, flashbacks in which the person feels or acts as though the trauma is happening again, and intense psychological or physical distress when confronted with reminders. Avoidance symptoms involve effortful avoidance of distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings about the event, as well as avoidance of external reminders like certain people, places, or conversations. Negative alterations in cognition and mood include an inability to remember important aspects of the event, persistent and exaggerated negative beliefs about oneself or the world, distorted blame directed at oneself or others, a persistently negative emotional state, loss of interest in activities, feelings of detachment from others, and an inability to experience positive emotions. Finally, alterations in arousal and reactivity include irritability or angry outbursts, reckless or self-destructive behavior, hypervigilance, an exaggerated startle response, difficulty concentrating, and sleep disturbance.

These symptoms must persist for more than one month and cause clinically significant distress or impairment for the diagnosis of PTSD to apply. This one month threshold is what separates PTSD from acute stress disorder, which describes a similar symptom picture in the first month after trauma, when many people are still in an early, often self-resolving, stress response.

An important and genuinely reassuring fact is that most people who are exposed to a traumatic event do not go on to develop PTSD. Vulnerability depends on a number of factors, including how severe and prolonged the trauma was, how directly life-threatening it felt, and the person's history before the event. This is where the connection to adverse childhood experiences becomes important: research consistently finds that childhood adversity, things like abuse, neglect, or a chaotic or frightening household, is associated with greater vulnerability to PTSD and other stress-related conditions later in life. One plausible explanation is that early adversity shapes the developing stress-response system and emotional regulation capacities in ways that leave a person more reactive to later threats, though this remains an active area of research rather than a fully settled mechanism.

PTSD's history is closely tied to the study of combat trauma. Diagnoses describing similar symptom patterns appeared under different names across earlier wars, and PTSD was formally added to the DSM in 1980, following extensive study of Vietnam War veterans. Combat exposure remains a well documented pathway to the disorder, but PTSD is by no means limited to it. It occurs after sexual assault, serious accidents, natural disasters, and witnessing violence, among other traumas, and the diagnostic criteria apply the same way regardless of the setting in which the trauma occurred.
